# Opening up a wall

A contractor's primer on taking out an interior wall.

## How to tell whether a wall is load-bearing

An exterior wall is always load-bearing. An interior wall probably is if it runs perpendicular to the floor or ceiling joists above it, sits directly over a beam or wall in the basement, or has a wall directly above it on the next floor. A wall that runs parallel to the joists is often a simple partition. Look in the basement and the attic before you decide.

## Beams and headers

When a load-bearing wall comes out, a beam must carry what the wall carried. A laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beam is common, sized by the span and the load above. The load is held on temporary support walls while the old wall is cut out, and the new beam bears on posts that continue down to the foundation.

## Plan, permit and engineer

Taking out a load-bearing wall needs a building permit and, almost always, a structural engineer's drawing for the beam size and posts. Plan on $500 to $1,000 for the engineer and several weeks for the permit.

## Non-bearing partitions

A partition wall carries only its own weight and can be removed with a pry bar and patience. Check for wiring, plumbing and ducts inside first.

## Wiring, pipes and ducts in a wall

Turn off the circuit before opening a wall. Wires and pipes in a removed wall must be rerouted, and a gas or hot-water pipe needs a licensed trade, and a permit.
